messages.content: I am organizing a two-day offsite for a team of twelve software engineers in late March. We have a budget of about 9,000 euros, and half of the team will travel from other cities. I want one day of planning work on next year's roadmap and one day of something more relaxed that still helps people who rarely meet in person get to know each other. Could you suggest a schedule for both days, a rough split of the budget, and a few things that usually go wrong at events like this, so that I can avoid them?

A water tank holds 1,200 liters. Pipe A fills the empty tank in 6 hours and pipe B fills it in 4 hours. A drain at the bottom empties a full tank in 8 hours. At 9:00 the tank is one quarter full, and someone opens pipe A and the drain. At 10:30 they also open pipe B. At what time is the tank full? Explain each step and check the answer.

Read this incident review and list the three action items that would have shortened this incident the most, with one sentence each on why.

Incident review: elevated write latency in the eu-west object storage cluster

Summary

On Tuesday between 09:12 and 13:47 UTC, the eu-west object storage cluster served write requests with elevated latency. The 99th percentile of PUT latency rose from a normal value of about 180 milliseconds to between 2.1 and 4.6 seconds. Read latency stayed within its normal range for most of the window. About 3.2 percent of PUT requests failed with a timeout at the load balancer, and clients that retried without backoff made the queue longer. No data was lost. Two internal teams paused their nightly backup jobs, and one external customer opened a priority ticket because their ingestion pipeline fell behind by about four hours.

The direct cause was a combination of two changes. First, a configuration change on Monday evening raised the number of concurrent compaction workers on each storage node from four to twelve. Second, the cluster received a planned increase in write traffic on Tuesday morning when a large customer started a migration. Together they saturated the write path of the NVMe devices on the nodes that held the busiest placement groups, and the journal flush time grew until request deadlines expired.

Timeline (all times UTC)

Monday 18:40. An engineer on the storage team merged a change that raised the compaction concurrency from four to twelve workers per node. The goal was to reduce the backlog of small objects that had accumulated after a previous incident. The change passed review and the canary stage, where it ran on three nodes for two hours with normal traffic.

Monday 21:05. The change reached all 96 nodes of the cluster through the standard rollout. Compaction throughput rose by a factor of about 2.6, and the backlog started to fall as intended. Write latency did not change at that time, because evening traffic is low.

Tuesday 08:30. The customer migration started. The customer had announced it two weeks earlier, and capacity planning had approved a peak of 40,000 PUT requests per second, about 35 percent above the normal morning peak.

Tuesday 09:12. The first latency alert fired for the 99th percentile of PUT latency above one second for five minutes. The on-call engineer acknowledged it at 09:15 and started to look at the storage cluster dashboards.

Tuesday 09:24. The engineer saw that the latency increase was limited to about one third of the nodes. Those nodes showed device utilization near 100 percent and journal flush times above 800 milliseconds. The engineer suspected a hardware problem on one rack, because the affected nodes were not spread evenly.

Tuesday 09:40. A second engineer joined. They checked the rack hypothesis and found that the affected nodes were in four different racks, so a shared hardware fault was unlikely. They noticed that the affected nodes held the primary copies of the placement groups that the migrating customer wrote to most.

Tuesday 10:05. The team asked the customer to reduce the migration rate. The customer reduced it by half at 10:20. Latency improved for about fifteen minutes and then rose again, because retry traffic from other clients filled the gap.

Tuesday 10:50. The incident commander opened a formal incident and paged the compaction owner. The compaction owner joined at 11:02 and pointed out the Monday change. The team then compared device statistics before and after the rollout and saw that background write bandwidth per node had grown from about 600 megabytes per second to about 1.6 gigabytes per second.

Tuesday 11:30. The team decided to roll back the compaction change instead of throttling it, because the rollback was a known and tested path. The rollback started at 11:41 and reached all nodes at 12:26, because the rollout system applies changes in batches of eight nodes with a health check after each batch.

Tuesday 12:40. Journal flush times returned to normal on most nodes. Six nodes still showed high latency, because their compaction workers did not stop until their current jobs finished. The team restarted the compaction service on those six nodes at 13:20.

Tuesday 13:47. Latency was back to normal for fifteen minutes and the incident was closed. The customer resumed the migration at full rate at 15:00 without further problems.

Impact

During the window, 3.2 percent of PUT requests failed and about 41 percent completed in more than one second. GET requests were mostly unaffected, but list operations on the busiest buckets slowed down because they read the same journals. The nightly backup jobs of two internal teams were delayed by one day. The external customer received a credit under the service level agreement.

Root cause analysis

Each storage node has four NVMe devices. Every write goes first to a journal on one device and then, in the background, into the main data files. Compaction reads small objects and rewrites them into larger files, so it creates both read and write load on the same devices. The write path of the devices has a sustained limit that is much lower than the burst limit that the specification sheet shows. Under sustained mixed load, the measured limit is about 2.2 gigabytes per second per device.

With four compaction workers, compaction used about 15 percent of that limit at peak. With twelve workers, it used about 45 percent. The migration traffic added foreground writes that concentrated on a small set of placement groups. On the nodes that held those groups, the sum of foreground and background writes passed the sustained limit. When the device stays above its limit, its internal garbage collection runs more often, and the latency of each write grows. The journal flush then waits for the slowest device, so the latency of every request on that node grows with it.

The canary did not show the problem, because canary traffic is normal production traffic on three nodes. It did not include a load test that combined compaction at the new concurrency with a peak in foreground writes. The capacity plan for the migration did not include background work, because the plan template only asks for foreground request rates.

The rollback took 45 minutes. The rollout system is built for safety, and its batch size and health checks are correct for most changes. For a change that makes the system worse under load, a slow rollback extends the incident. The system has an emergency mode that applies a change to all nodes at once, but nobody on the call remembered how to enable it.

Retries made the incident longer. Several clients retried timed-out PUT requests immediately and without a limit. That behavior doubled the request rate on the affected nodes for most of the window. Our client libraries implement exponential backoff with jitter, but two internal services use an older library version that does not.

What went well

The alerting fired within minutes of the first latency increase. The team found the set of affected nodes quickly.

What went badly

The first hypothesis, a rack fault, cost about 25 minutes. The compaction change was not visible on the incident dashboard, so the team did not connect it to the latency until the compaction owner joined. The rollback was slow. The capacity plan ignored background load.

Action items

1. Add recent configuration changes to the incident dashboard, with the time of the last rollout stage for each change. Owner: observability team. Due in two weeks.
2. Add a sustained mixed-load test to the canary stage for changes to compaction, scrubbing, and rebalancing. The test must run the new configuration at the planned peak foreground rate for at least thirty minutes. Owner: storage team. Due in four weeks.
3. Change the capacity plan template so that it asks for background work on the same devices, and add the current compaction, scrub, and rebalance bandwidth to the planning dashboard. Owner: capacity planning. Due in three weeks.
4. Document the emergency rollout mode in the runbook, and practice it in the next game day. Owner: release engineering. Due in two weeks.
5. Make compaction concurrency adaptive. Compaction should measure the journal flush time and reduce its workers when the flush time passes a threshold. Owner: storage team. Due in eight weeks.
6. Upgrade the two internal services to the client library version with exponential backoff and jitter, and add a server-side retry budget per client. Owner: platform team. Due in four weeks.
7. Add device-level sustained write bandwidth to the node health score, so that the placement system can move hot placement groups away from saturated nodes. Owner: storage team. Due in ten weeks.

Open questions

The team does not yet know why compaction on six nodes continued after the rollback. The compaction service should stop new jobs within one minute of a configuration change, but on those nodes it started new jobs for another forty minutes. One theory is that those nodes had a large queue of jobs that were already assigned, and the service only checks the configuration when it requests new work.

We also need to decide whether the sustained write limit of 2.2 gigabytes per second should be a hard limit in the scheduler or only an alert. A hard limit protects latency but can let the compaction backlog grow without bound during long traffic peaks.

Here is a design proposal from our platform team. Summarize it in a short paragraph, and then give your two strongest concerns about the design.

Design proposal: tiered retention for application logs

Status: draft for review by the platform architecture group.

Background

Our services write about 38 terabytes of structured application logs per day. All logs go to one search cluster and stay there for thirty days. The cluster has 140 nodes with fast local SSDs. It costs more than any other part of the observability platform, and its cost grows by about 4 percent each month because new services add logs faster than old services remove them.

Most log reads are recent. In the last quarter, 86 percent of queries asked for data from the last 24 hours, 11 percent asked for data from the last seven days, and only 3 percent asked for older data. The older queries come from three groups: security investigations, audits that need a record of user actions, and engineers who debug a problem that started weeks before somebody noticed it. These queries are rare, but they matter, and some of them have legal deadlines.

At the same time, about 60 percent of the stored bytes are debug and info messages that nobody reads after the first day. Teams log at these levels because the cost of a log line is invisible to them, and because it is hard to know in advance which line will help during an incident.

Goals

1. Reduce the cost of log storage by at least 40 percent within two quarters without losing the ability to answer the rare older queries.
2. Keep the query experience for the last seven days the same as today: the same query language, the same interface, and a 95th percentile query time below three seconds.
3. Give teams a clear view of what their logs cost, so that they can make informed choices.
4. Keep audit logs for one year, as the compliance team now requires, instead of thirty days.

Non-goals

This proposal does not change how services produce logs or the log format. It does not replace the search cluster with another product. It does not cover metrics or traces, which have their own storage systems.

Proposed design

We split storage into three tiers by age.

The hot tier keeps the last seven days in the existing search cluster. Because it holds seven days instead of thirty, we can reduce the cluster from 140 to about 50 nodes, even after we leave room for growth and for node failures.

The warm tier keeps days eight to thirty in compressed columnar files in object storage. A query service reads these files directly and supports the same query language for the common filters: time range, service name, log level, trace identifier, and free text search on the message field. Free text search in the warm tier is slower, because it has no full index. Instead, each file has a small summary with the set of services, the levels, and a bloom filter of the tokens in the message field. The query service uses the summaries to skip files that cannot match, and scans the rest in parallel.

The cold tier keeps audit logs for one year, and all other logs for ninety days, in the same file format in a cheaper storage class. Cold queries run as batch jobs. A user submits a query and receives the result by email or in a shared folder, usually within an hour.

A daily job moves data from the hot tier to the warm tier. It reads the indices of the day that leaves the hot tier, writes the columnar files and their summaries, checks that the row counts match, and only then deletes the indices. A second daily job moves files from the warm storage class to the cold storage class, and deletes files that are past their retention time.

Query service

The query service is stateless and runs as a pool of workers behind the existing query gateway. The gateway sends the part of a query that covers the last seven days to the hot tier and the part that covers older days to the query service, then merges the results in time order. Each worker reads the summaries of all files in the requested time range first, which takes a few hundred milliseconds even for a month of data, because the summaries are small and cached in memory. It then assigns the remaining files to scan tasks of similar size. A query stops early when it has found the number of results that the user asked for, which is the common case for searches that look for the first occurrence of an error. Every query has a limit on the bytes it may scan, and the user sees an estimate of the scan size before a large query starts. The service records the scanned bytes, the number of skipped files, and the query time for each query, so that we can tune the file size and the summaries after launch. Workers hold no data between queries, so the pool can grow during an incident, when many engineers search at the same time, and shrink again at night.

Sampling of debug logs

In addition to the tiers, we propose to sample debug logs after the first day. The hot tier keeps all debug lines. When a day moves to the warm tier, the job keeps all debug lines that share a trace identifier with an error or warning line, and keeps one in ten of the other debug lines. Teams can turn sampling off for a service when they have a reason, and they see the cost of that choice on their dashboard.

Cost estimate

The finance team helped us compare the current cost with the proposed design. We use list prices and our current discount. The hot tier with 50 nodes costs about 36 percent of today's cluster. The warm tier, with an expected compression ratio of eight to one and with sampling, adds about 9 percent. The cold tier adds about 4 percent, including one year of audit logs. The query service adds about 3 percent. The total is about 52 percent of today's cost, a reduction of 48 percent. If the compression ratio is only five to one, the reduction is 43 percent, which still meets the goal.

Risks

The warm query service is new code, and slow warm queries could frustrate engineers during an incident. We will run the warm tier in shadow mode for one month, answering every query from both systems and comparing results and times, before we shrink the hot cluster.

The move job could lose data if it deletes indices before the files are complete. The job deletes an index only after it checks row counts and the checksums of the uploaded files, and the object storage bucket keeps deleted files for seven days.

Sampling could remove a debug line that would have explained an incident. The rule that keeps all lines that share a trace identifier with an error or warning reduces this risk. We will also keep all debug lines for the first day, when most debugging happens.

Teams could react to the cost dashboard by removing logs that the security team needs. The security team will review changes to log levels for services that handle user data.

Alternatives considered

We considered keeping thirty days in a smaller search cluster with cheaper disks. This saves about 20 percent but does not meet the goal, and it does not give us one year of audit logs.

We considered a managed log service from our cloud provider. Its price for our volume is close to our current cost, and moving the query interface would affect every team.

We considered aggressive sampling at the source. This saves the most, but it removes data before anybody knows whether it is useful, and services would need code changes.

Rollout plan

Phase one builds the move job and the warm query service, and runs them in shadow mode for one month. Phase two reduces the hot retention to fourteen days and then to seven days, while we watch query times and user feedback. Phase three enables debug sampling for services that opt in, then for all services with a two-week notice. Phase four shrinks the hot cluster. Each phase has a rollback path, and we will not start a phase until the previous one has run for two weeks without a regression.

Questions for reviewers

Is seven days the right size for the hot tier, or should we keep fourteen days because some teams run weekly reports? Should the cold tier accept interactive queries for audit logs, at a higher cost, because auditors sometimes need answers within a day?
